lesson.title: Treble Filters: Letting the High End Through with a High-Pass Circuit
lesson.summary: A treble filter is a high-pass filter tuned to the upper end of the audio signal, passing treble frequencies while attenuating the bass and midrange below it.
lesson.body:
A high-pass filter does the mirror image of a low-pass filter: it passes frequencies above its cutoff largely unchanged while attenuating frequencies below that cutoff. A treble filter is a high-pass filter applied to an audio signal and tuned so its cutoff sits near the treble sub band, roughly 4,000 Hz to 20,000 Hz, so the crisp high frequency content of the signal, cymbals, sibilance, upper harmonics, passes through while the bass and midrange below it are rolled off.

The same cutoff frequency formula applies to a simple RC high-pass filter: fc = 1 / (2 times pi times R times C). Suppose a designer wants a treble filter with a cutoff near 4,000 Hz, at the low edge of the treble sub band. Choosing a resistor of R = 4 kilohms and a capacitor of C = 0.01 microfarads, which is 10 nanofarads, gives fc = 1 / (2 times pi times 4,000 times 0.00000001) = 1 / (2 times pi times 0.00004) = 1 / 0.0002513 = 3,979 Hz, which rounds to about 4 kHz, confirming the component choice matches the intended cutoff.

Just like the bass filter, a strict high-pass treble filter eventually attenuates the bass and midrange almost completely, which is useful for isolating a tweeter but too extreme for a simple treble knob. Tone control circuits again use a shelving version of this idea, one that levels off at a controlled amount of cut or boost above the cutoff rather than removing the lower frequencies outright. With both the bass filter and the treble filter now defined, the next section shows how they combine into a single, adjustable tone control.
